newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana fails to approve New Orleans casino plan.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana fails to approve New Orleans casino plan.

text.p: Louisiana's Legislature adjourned Monday night without approving the bankruptcy reorganization plan for the state's land-based casino in New Orleans, leaving the casino's future murky.

Harrah's Jazz Co, a consortium of 10 local investors, what was then Harrah's Hotel Casinos (owned by Promus Hotel Corp) and developer Christopher Hemeter, has been mired in bankruptcy proceedings since November 1995.

In April, a federal bankruptcy court judge confirmed the company's plan for reorganization. The plan was approved by the Louisiana Gaming Control Commission, the New Orleans City Council and Gov. Mike Foster but ran into stiff opposition in the Legislature, which adjourned without taking final action on the proposal.

Supporters of the reorganization still may try to obtain legislative approval through a mail ballot. The federal bankruptcy court judge could order the plan to proceed. Or the state could be allowed to solicit bids to operate the casino from Harrah's competitors.

Under the reorganization plan, the casino company would emerge as a new company called Jazz Casino Co. In exchange for their $435 million in junk bond debt, bondholders would receive $187 million in new bonds and slightly more than 50 percent of the new company's stock.
Forty percent of the remaining ownership would be controlled by Harrah's Entertainment Inc, and a group of private investors would control the rest.
Unsecured creditors, the largest of which is general contractor Centex-Landis, would be paid in full for claims totaling about $105 million.

Some legislators object to the state continuing to do business with Harrah's, saying the company was deceitful in publicly denying that the project was in trouble just before declaring bankruptcy and laying off 3,000 workers. Other opponents want Harrah's Entertainment to guarantee a required $100 million annual payment to the state for the duration of the exclusive 20-year state lease.

The legislature in 1992 approved one land-based casino in Louisiana, with a 20-year monopoly, to be opened on land owned by the city of New Orleans near the Mississippi River and the historic French Quarter.

The project has been mired in regulatory problems, inter- governmental squabbling, partisan politics and litigation since it's inception. A temporary casino that finally opened in May 1995 closed just five months later as Harrah's Jazz sought bankruptcy protection.
